title: AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
description: A complete practice subject: Prelim, Midterm, Semifinals and Finals. Eight lessons, eight one-question quizzes, four activities and four written examinations. Original classroom exercises; replace with your approved syllabus before institutional use.

overview.title: Course guide
overview.body:
AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Practice subject template | Original Academy content | Not an approved institutional syllabus.

Outcomes
O1. Explain an engineering problem, its constraints and the evidence needed.
O2. Use consistent units and trace calculations.
O3. Interpret a simple force model and stated assumptions.
O4. Compare materials and resources using supplied data.
O5. Evaluate uncertainty and communicate a defensible recommendation.

Study route
Prelim (weeks 1-4): engineering practice, evidence and units.
Midterm (weeks 5-8): forces, motion and model limits.
Semifinals (weeks 9-12): materials, resources and trade-offs.
Finals (weeks 13-16): integrated design brief, validation and reporting.
Each period: Lesson A, Quiz A, Lesson B, Quiz B, Activity, Examination.

Assessment
8 quizzes: one multiple-choice question each, automatically scored out of 1.
4 activities: written outputs, instructor-rated out of 100 using the stated rubric.
4 examinations: four written problems each, instructor-rated out of 100.
Review before submitting: one submission per item version. Do your own work; cite any outside sources.

Suggested planning weights: quizzes 20%, activities 30%, examinations 50%. Use category averages if applying these weights manually. Confirm your institution's policy first; the app does not calculate a weighted course grade or infer passing readiness. Reading completion is self-reported and is separate from achievement.

Instructor preparation
Review objectives, sequence, source permissions, accessibility and rubrics. Replace synthetic data with suitable approved classroom cases; verify any outside links as the student. Set enrollment eligibility, publish, then test with the student account. Return clear feedback before the next period.
No aircraft operation, maintenance release or real flight is authorized by these exercises.

entries.title: Prelim - Lesson 1: Engineering evidence
entries.body:
Outcome O1: distinguish a requirement, evidence and an assumption.
An engineering brief states what a solution must achieve, the limits it must respect and how success will be checked. A requirement is testable; an assumption is a condition taken as true until checked. A measurement is useful evidence only when its method, units and limits are known.
Classroom case: a model-aircraft storage rack must hold six models within a supplied floor-space limit. 'Looks strong' is not an acceptance criterion. 'Supports the stated classroom load without permanent deformation in the specified test' identifies a measurable outcome, but the instructor must define the load, setup and limits.
Record the document title, revision and source before using a table. Conflicting versions require clarification rather than silent mixing.
Practice: write one requirement, one assumption and one evidence item for the storage-rack brief. Identify what you would ask the instructor before calculating.

entries.title: Prelim - Quiz 1: Evidence
entries.body: Which statement is a testable requirement for a classroom model carrier?
options: It must carry the specified classroom load within the stated deflection limit.
It will probably be strong enough.
The material is assumed to be perfect.

entries.title: Prelim - Lesson 2: Units and records
entries.body:
Outcome O2: convert units and show a traceable calculation.
Write the quantity, symbol and unit before substituting numbers. A calculation should allow another student to follow the input data, conversion, equation and conclusion.
Worked example: 2.4 m = 2400 mm because 1 m = 1000 mm. Show the conversion factor so units cancel. Do not add a length in metres directly to a length recorded in millimetres.
Synthetic dataset: lengths 1200 mm, 0.8 m and 50 cm. Express each in metres before adding them. Report an appropriate number of digits rather than implying greater precision than the inputs provide.
A useful calculation record includes the data source or supplied dataset, assumptions, steps, units and one reasonableness check. Correct arithmetic with the wrong unit is still an incorrect result.
Practice: prepare a conversion table and explain how a unit error could change a classroom decision.

entries.title: Prelim - Quiz 2: Unit conversion
entries.body: A drawing gives a span of 1500 mm. What is the span in metres?

entries.title: Prelim - Activity 1: Requirement and calculation record
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O2 | Individual written output | 300-450 words plus calculations.
Use this fictional brief: store six classroom models; each model has a supplied mass of 0.75 kg; available rack width is 1.2 m. This is a planning exercise, not a structural design authorization.
Submit: (1) three measurable requirements, (2) an input/units table, (3) total model mass, (4) width in millimetres, (5) two assumptions and the evidence needed to check them, and (6) one independent reasonableness check.
Do not select a real load rating from this exercise.
Rubric /100: requirements 25; calculations and units 30; assumptions/evidence 25; clear traceable record 20.

entries.title: Prelim - Examination 1
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O2 | Individual written examination | Four questions, 25 points each.
Q1. A brief says 'build an efficient model carrier'. Rewrite it as two testable requirements. Identify one missing numerical limit without inventing it.
Q2. Convert 1750 mm and 65 cm to metres, then find their combined length. Show unit cancellation.
Q3. A classroom inventory contains eight models of 0.625 kg each. Calculate their total mass. State one assumption and one check on the result.
Q4. Two worksheets show different values for the same dimension. Describe a documented process for resolving the discrepancy before calculation.
Submit one numbered response. Suggested duration: 60 minutes; the app does not enforce a timer.
Each question /25: sound reasoning 10; correct method/evidence 8; units or explicit assumptions 4; clear presentation 3. No automatic written grading.

entries.title: Midterm - Lesson 3: Simple force models
entries.body:
Outcome O3: interpret a stated force model.
Use a free-body diagram to identify the forces acting on the object being studied. State the positive direction, magnitude and unit for each force. A force balance describes the model under its assumptions; it does not prove that a real aircraft is safe.
Worked classroom example: two horizontal forces of 12 N and 7 N act in opposite directions on a model cart. If right is positive and 12 N acts right, the net force is +5 N.
For an idealized aircraft in steady, level, unaccelerated flight, the simplified model balances lift with weight and thrust with drag. Changing the assumptions can change the balance.
Practice: sketch arrows for a cart pulled right by 18 N against a leftward 11 N resistance. Explain what the model leaves out and what further data would be needed to predict acceleration.

entries.title: Midterm - Quiz 3: Resultant force
entries.body: A model cart has 20 N acting right and 8 N acting left. What is the net horizontal force?

entries.title: Midterm - Lesson 4: Motion and assumptions
entries.body:
Outcomes O2-O3: relate distance, time and average speed under stated conditions.
Average speed equals total distance divided by elapsed time. It is not automatically the speed at every instant. Define the interval and use consistent units.
Worked example: a model cart covers 24 m in 6 s. Its average speed is 4 m/s. This observation alone does not establish constant speed or acceleration.
Synthetic observations: trial A covers 30 m in 10 s; trial B covers 42 m in 12 s. Compare average speeds and list two measurement limitations, such as timing resolution and distance marking.
A model should be checked against evidence. If a measured result differs from a prediction, review assumptions, inputs, method and measurement uncertainty before changing a convenient number.
Practice: describe a repeatable classroom measurement method and explain why repeating a trial can reveal variability.

entries.title: Midterm - Quiz 4: Average speed
entries.body: A model cart travels 45 m in 15 s. What is its average speed?

entries.title: Midterm - Activity 2: Model and measurement
entries.body:
Outcomes O2-O3 | Individual written output | 350-500 words plus a labelled sketch.
Use only this supplied model: horizontal pull 16 N right, resistance 10 N left; measured travel 36 m in 12 s.
Submit: (1) a text-described or externally linked free-body sketch with positive direction, (2) net force, (3) average speed, (4) three model/measurement assumptions, and (5) a repeatable validation plan with one rejection condition.
Do not infer acceleration from speed alone; identify missing data. A labelled text diagram is acceptable because the app accepts written output.
Rubric /100: model representation 25; calculations/units 30; assumptions and limits 20; validation plan 25.

entries.title: Midterm - Examination 2
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O3 | Individual written examination | Four questions, 25 points each.
Q1. Describe the four named forces in the simplified steady-level-flight model and state the balances assumed by that model.
Q2. A cart has 28 N rightward pull and 13 N leftward resistance. Determine the net force using a declared sign convention.
Q3. Trial A covers 64 m in 16 s; trial B covers 75 m in 15 s. Find each average speed and compare them with units.
Q4. A student claims these average speeds prove constant speed throughout each trial. Evaluate the claim and propose the extra evidence needed.
Submit numbered reasoning and calculations. Suggested duration: 60 minutes; no app-enforced timer.
Each question /25: reasoning 10; correct method/evidence 8; units or assumptions 4; clarity 3.

entries.title: Semifinals - Lesson 5: Material comparisons
entries.body:
Outcome O4: compare alternatives using the same basis.
A comparison is meaningful when candidates meet the same stated function and constraints. Mass alone does not establish strength, durability, suitability or approval.
For a supplied volume, estimated mass equals density multiplied by volume. Keep units consistent.
Worked example: an imaginary classroom material with density 1200 kg/m3 occupying 0.002 m3 has estimated mass 2.4 kg. This arithmetic is not a qualification of the material.
Synthetic candidates for the same 0.001 m3 component: P has density 1600 kg/m3 and supplied cost PHP 180; Q has density 2400 kg/m3 and cost PHP 140. These fictional figures are task inputs, not market prices.
Practice: calculate both masses, compare the trade-off and identify missing strength/manufacturing data before recommending either candidate.

entries.title: Semifinals - Quiz 5: Mass estimate
entries.body: A fictional material has density 1500 kg/m3 and volume 0.002 m3. What is its estimated mass?

entries.title: Semifinals - Lesson 6: Resource decisions
entries.body:
Outcomes O1/O4: justify a decision under explicit constraints.
Start with non-negotiable requirements, then compare eligible alternatives. A low cost does not compensate for failing a required limit. Show which evidence supports each judgment.
Synthetic procurement exercise: option A costs PHP 240 per unit and needs 2 hours assembly; option B costs PHP 200 per unit and needs 3 hours. Four units are needed. The classroom budget is PHP 1000 and assembly allowance is 10 hours. These figures are fictional.
Calculate total cost and time for each option. Identify which meets both limits, then state what remains unverified. A decision matrix can use columns for requirement, supplied evidence, pass/fail and uncertainty.
Practice: explain how your recommendation changes if the budget becomes PHP 850. If neither option meets all limits, request a revised brief rather than claiming success.

entries.title: Semifinals - Quiz 6: Constraint check
entries.body: Four kits cost PHP 220 each. With a PHP 1000 budget, how much budget remains?

entries.title: Semifinals - Activity 3: Evidence-based selection
entries.body:
Outcomes O1/O2/O4 | Individual written output | 400-600 words plus a comparison table.
Fictional candidates for one classroom model support:
P: density 1800 kg/m3, volume 0.001 m3, cost PHP 450, assembly 2 h.
Q: density 2500 kg/m3, volume 0.001 m3, cost PHP 380, assembly 4 h.
Constraints: estimated mass no more than 2 kg, cost no more than PHP 500, assembly no more than 3 h.
Submit masses, a requirement/evidence/pass-fail table, a recommendation, three missing evidence items and one sensitivity check with a changed limit. Treat material figures as supplied data, not real certification properties.
Rubric /100: calculations 25; constraint matrix 30; justified recommendation 25; uncertainty and sensitivity 20.

entries.title: Semifinals - Examination 3
entries.body:
Outcomes O1/O2/O4 | Individual written examination | Four questions, 25 points each.
Q1. Estimate mass for a fictional component of volume 0.0015 m3 and supplied density 2000 kg/m3. Show units.
Q2. Six kits cost PHP 175 each. Find total cost and compare with the fictional PHP 1100 budget.
Q3. Candidate A has mass 1.8 kg and cost PHP 600; B has mass 2.2 kg and cost PHP 450. Limits are 2 kg and PHP 550. Explain whether either qualifies and identify the next decision.
Q4. Explain why selecting the lowest-density candidate alone is insufficient for a real engineering recommendation. List four additional evidence categories.
Submit numbered responses. Suggested duration: 60 minutes; no app-enforced timer.
Each question /25: reasoning 10; correct method/evidence 8; units or assumptions 4; clarity 3.

entries.title: Finals - Lesson 7: Integration and validation
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O5: connect a brief to a defensible test plan.
A useful engineering report links each requirement to evidence and a stated acceptance criterion. Separate predicted, measured and unverified results. A successful drawing or calculation does not establish field performance.
For a fictional classroom model carrier, plan checks for capacity, dimensions, estimated mass, cost and documentation quality. Define the setup, inputs, observation and pass/fail rule for each check. State who reviews unresolved assumptions.
Worked planning example: 'Compare the measured width with the supplied maximum using the stated measuring method; record the value and uncertainty.' The numerical limit must come from the brief, not an arbitrary change made after the result.
Practice: prepare a requirement-to-test table and explain what you would do when a required check is unavailable. Report it as unverified rather than passed.

entries.title: Finals - Quiz 7: Verification evidence
entries.body: A design calculation passes, but the required physical check has not been performed. Which report statement is appropriate?
options: The missing check can be marked passed.
Calculation reviewed; physical check not tested.
No assumptions need to be recorded.

entries.title: Finals - Lesson 8: Technical communication
entries.body:
Outcome O5: communicate a recommendation with traceable limits.
Lead with the recommendation, then show the requirement, evidence and reasoning that support it. Include units, input sources, assumptions, uncertainty, unresolved checks and the next action. Use a concise table when comparing alternatives.
A report should let another person reproduce the analysis without guessing what a number means. Keep document revisions and distinguish original work from borrowed material.
When evidence is incomplete, make a conditional recommendation. Explain which additional result could change the decision; do not use confident language to conceal a missing check.
Practice: rewrite 'The carrier is perfect' as a bounded conclusion that identifies what was reviewed, what was measured and what remains unverified. Review a peer's fictional report for a missing unit, unsupported assumption and unclear acceptance criterion.

entries.title: Finals - Quiz 8: Reporting
entries.body: Which conclusion gives the most useful engineering decision record?
options: It is the best because it looks good.
The recommendation is final even without evidence.
The cheapest option is always acceptable.
Candidate P meets the supplied limits; the listed untested checks remain pending.

entries.title: Finals - Activity 4: Integrated subject portfolio
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O5 | Individual written output | 600-900 words with tables.
Fictional model carrier brief: hold four classroom models of 0.8 kg each; carrier width no more than 900 mm; planning budget PHP 1200. Candidate P: width 0.85 m, cost PHP 1100, carrier mass 1.6 kg. Candidate Q: width 0.95 m, cost PHP 950, carrier mass 1.3 kg. No load-test evidence is supplied.
Submit: requirements and units table; total model mass and total carried mass for each candidate; pass/fail matrix for the supplied dimensional/budget limits; conditional recommendation; four-check validation plan; unresolved evidence; reflection on one earlier feedback point.
Do not claim load-carrying safety from these figures. This is an academic planning portfolio.
Rubric /100: requirements and traceability 20; calculations 25; comparison/recommendation 25; validation and limits 20; reflection and clarity 10.

entries.title: Finals - Examination 4
entries.body:
Outcomes O1-O5 | Individual cumulative written examination | Four questions, 25 points each.
Q1. A fictional carrier holds five models of 0.6 kg each and has mass 1.2 kg. Calculate model mass and combined mass; state what those numbers do not establish.
Q2. Candidate A: width 0.88 m, cost PHP 1050; B: width 940 mm, cost PHP 900. Limits: width 900 mm and cost PHP 1100. Compare both on the same units and justify a provisional choice.
Q3. For that choice, write three measurable verification checks, giving the setup, evidence and pass/fail criterion. Identify missing inputs rather than inventing safety limits.
Q4. Write a concise recommendation that separates calculations, supplied data, assumptions and untested physical behavior. Describe how a failed required check changes the recommendation.
Submit one numbered response. Suggested duration: 90 minutes; no app-enforced timer.
Each question /25: reasoning 10; correct method/evidence 8; units or assumptions 4; clarity 3.
